svg.text: Business rules make or save the business money; strictly, they would do so even if executed manually (a bank charging N% interest on a loan, whether a program or a
clerk with an abacus calculates it)
Entity (Critical Business Rules and Data)
critical rules exist even without automation and need data (a loan's balance,
interest rate and payment schedule); bound together as an object holding the data
or with easy access to it, whose interface is the critical rules (Fig 20.1); pure
business: no databases, user interfaces or frameworks; no OO language needed, just
one separate module
Use case (application-specific rules)
describes how an automated system is used: the input, output and processing steps;
makes sense only in a system (loan officers may not give payment estimates until
contact information is validated and the credit score is 500 or higher); mentions
the Customer entity (Fig 20.2); controls the dance of the Entities; says nothing of
web, thick client, console or service
Use case
knows
Entities (higher level)
Use case
Dependency
use cases depend on Entities, not the reverse: entities are general, farther from
inputs and outputs, so higher level
Request and response models
a use case takes simple request structures and returns simple response structures,
independent of HttpRequest, HttpResponse, HTML or SQL; do not embed Entity
references (different reasons to change: tramp data and conditionals)
Conclusion
business rules are why the system exists, the family jewels: keep them pristine,
the heart of the system and the most independent, reusable code, with lesser
concerns plugged in
